rows.reference: Apply a tourniquet 5 to 7 centimetres above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops. Write the time on the skin. Do not remove it in the field. Lay them down, keep them warm and still, and watch for shock.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If the bleeding has still not slowed after ten minutes, apply more direct pressure to the wound. If the bleeding continues, repeat the process. If the person is in shock or showing signs of distress, such as pale, cold, or clammy skin, seek emergency medical help immediately.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If the bleeding has persisted for ten minutes without improvement, apply additional pressure for 10–20 minutes. If the bleeding continues, repeat the process. If the person becomes unconscious or shows signs of shock, begin CPR immediately.

rows.reference: Press a clean cloth or folded pad firmly onto the wound with the heel of your hand. Do not lift it to check. If it soaks through, add another on top. Maintain pressure at least 10 minutes. Raise the limb unless a fracture is suspected. If bleeding continues, apply a tourniquet.
rows.train_prompt_answer: To apply direct pressure, place the injured area on a firm surface, lean the person slightly forward, and apply firm but gentle pressure to the wound using your hand or a clean cloth. This helps control the bleeding by applying pressure to the site of the injury.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: To apply direct pressure, place the injured limb on a firm surface, lean it slightly towards the injured area, and apply firm but gentle pressure with your hand or a clean cloth. This helps control the bleeding by applying pressure to the site of the injury.

rows.reference: Lifting a soaked dressing tears off the forming clot, and clotting is how bleeding stops, so the wound rebleeds and restarts from zero. It also introduces contamination. Add a second dressing on top and maintain firm pressure. Do not remove a dressing once applied.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Lifting the dressing can cause more harm than good. It can disturb the dressing's adhesive, expose the wound to contaminants, and increase the risk of infection. Always replace the dressing gently and carefully.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Lifting a blood-saturated dressing can cause more harm than good. It may disturb the clotting process, increase the risk of infection, and expose the wound to further contamination. Always replace the dressing gently and carefully.

rows.reference: Clean with soap and water. Sterilise fine-pointed tweezers with alcohol or a flame and let them cool. Grip the splinter close to the skin and pull it out at the angle it entered. Do not dig, squeeze or break it. Clean again and cover with a dressing. Seek care if deep, broken below the surface, or infected.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a small splinter is embedded in the shallow skin, it is important to sterilize the area and gently attempt to remove the splinter with a pair of tweezers or a splinter remover. If the splinter is too deep or difficult to remove, seek medical help for proper removal.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If the splinter is small and shallow, it can be removed with a pair of tweezers or a splinter remover. If it's too difficult to remove, you can use a sterile needle to push the splinter further into the skin and then pull it out. After removal, clean the area and apply a sterile dressing. If the area becomes infected or swollen, seek medical attention.

rows.reference: Do not remove the object; removing it can cause sudden heavy bleeding. Build padding around it on both sides, then bandage over the padding without pressing deeper. Do not press on the object. Immobilise the area. Lay them down, keep them still and warm, and watch for shock.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a person has an embedded foreign object, do not attempt to remove it yourself. This could cause further injury or damage to the surrounding tissues. Cover the wound with a sterile dressing and seek immediate medical attention.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If a person has an embedded foreign object, do not attempt to remove it yourself. This could cause further injury or damage to the surrounding tissue. Cover the wound with a clean dressing and apply pressure to stop bleeding. Seek emergency medical help immediately.

rows.reference: Suspect internal bleeding if the abdomen is tender, rigid or distended; there is bruising over the abdomen, flanks or groin; the person coughs or vomits blood or passes blood in urine; or shock develops with no visible wound. Lay them flat, raise the legs unless spinal or leg injury is suspected, keep them still and warm. Give nothing to eat or drink. Evacuate fast.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs that a person may be bleeding internally after trauma include vomiting blood, passing black or red stools, signs of shock (such as pale, cold, and clammy skin), and signs of internal injury such as swelling or bruising. Immediate medical attention is critical in such cases.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs that a person may be bleeding internally after trauma include severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood, signs of shock (such as pale, cold, or clammy skin), and signs of shock, such as rapid breathing or unconsciousness. Immediate first aid should be provided to control bleeding and seek medical help.

rows.reference: Movement raises heart rate and blood pressure, which can dislodge a forming clot. Cold constricts peripheral vessels, diverts blood from vital organs, and impairs clotting directly. Stillness protects the clot and lowers demand on a compromised circulation; warmth keeps clotting working. Together they slow hypovolaemic shock.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Keeping the casualty warm and still helps slow down the bleeding by maintaining blood flow to vital organs. It also reduces the risk of further complications, such as shock or organ damage.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Keeping a casualty with significant bleeding warm and still is important because it helps slow down the bleeding and reduces the risk of shock. It also helps maintain their body temperature, which is crucial for proper circulation and breathing.

rows.reference: Start CPR now. Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, the other interlocked on top. Compress at least 5 centimetres at 100 to 120 per minute with full recoil. Give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions if willing and able; otherwise compress continuously. Send anyone present for an AED. Continue until signs of life or help arrives.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If an adult collapses, is unresponsive and not breathing normally, immediately check for signs of breathing. If there is no breathing, start CPR immediately. If the person is breathing but unconscious, place them in the lateral position to maintain an open airway and seek medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If an adult collapses, is unresponsive and not breathing normally, immediately check for signs of breathing by placing your ear near their mouth and watching for chest rise and fall. If there is no breathing, begin CPR immediately, focusing on chest compressions and rescue breaths.

rows.reference: Check the scene is safe. Tap the shoulders and shout. If no response, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasping is not normal breathing. If breathing is not normal, start CPR. Do not delay CPR to check a pulse.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs of life include breathing, movement, or a pulse. If the person is not breathing or has no pulse, begin CPR immediately. If they are breathing but unconscious, continue CPR until help arrives.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs of life include breathing, movement, or a pulse. If the person is not breathing or has no pulse, begin CPR immediately. If they are breathing but unconscious, place them in the recovery position and continue monitoring their condition.

rows.reference: Effective compressions depress the chest at least 5 centimetres with full recoil each time; keep hands in contact but release pressure completely between compressions. Rate 100 to 120 per minute, about two per second. Depth falls as the rescuer tires, so swap every two minutes if possible. Keep interruptions under 10 seconds.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs that CPR chest compression is being performed effectively include the chest rising and falling with each compression, the casualty's pulse becoming weaker, and the casualty becoming more responsive. If these signs are not present, continue compressions and seek medical help immediately.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs that CPR chest compression is being performed effectively include the casualty's chest rising and falling with each compression, the casualty' breathing becoming shallower, and the rescuer feeling resistance as they apply pressure. If these signs are present, continue compressions and seek help as soon as possible.

rows.reference: Turn the AED on and follow its prompts. Place pads on bare dry skin, one below the right collarbone, one on the left chest below the armpit. Ensure nobody touches the person during analysis. If a shock is advised, warn everyone, confirm no contact, then shock. Resume compressions immediately.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If an AED arrives during a rescue, follow the voice prompts and begin chest compressions immediately. Continue until professional medical help arrives or the person shows signs of life.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If an AED arrives during a rescue, follow the device's voice instructions and place the pads on the chest of the victim. Begin chest compressions immediately and continue until professional help arrives.

rows.reference: Stopping compressions drops coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure to zero immediately, and it takes several seconds to rebuild it. Frequent pauses therefore cut resuscitation effectiveness. Pulse checks are also unreliable: rescuers and clinicians alike misjudge them under stress. The cost of the pause is certain; the value of the check is not.
rows.train_prompt_answer: It is recommended to check for pulses every 2-4 minutes to maintain the rhythm and effectiveness of the chest compressions. Stopping too frequently can lead to fatigue or injury to the rescuer.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: It is recommended to check for pulses every 2–4 minutes to maintain a consistent rhythm and avoid fatigue. Stopping too frequently can lead to reduced effectiveness and missed signs of life.

rows.reference: Start CPR immediately: 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, at least 5 centimetres deep, 100 to 120 per minute. With no way to call for help, stay and keep compressing; leaving the patient more than 10 seconds sharply reduces survival. For a child, give 2 minutes of CPR before briefly leaving to signal.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If there is no signal, call emergency services immediately and begin CPR immediately. If possible, use a mobile phone to call for help or ask someone nearby to call. Continue CPR until help arrives or the person starts breathing.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If there is no access to phone signal, use your best judgment to assess the situation. If the person is breathing and has a pulse, start CPR immediately. If they are not breathing or have no pulse, begin CPR with chest compressions and rescue breaths. Continue until help arrives or the person shows signs of life.

rows.reference: Give nothing to eat or drink. Do not induce vomiting. Note the time swallowed and the object type. A button battery in the oesophagus burns tissue within 2 hours; magnets attract through bowel walls and can perforate. Both need urgent endoscopy. Get the child to a facility capable of emergency endoscopy fast.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a young child has swallowed a button battery, it is a medical emergency. Do not give them anything to eat or drink, and seek immediate medical help. The child may require surgery to remove the object safely.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If a young child has swallowed a button battery, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention. Do not attempt to induce vomiting, as this could cause further injury. Keep the child calm and monitor their breathing and pulse. If the child is conscious, give them small sips of water if they are alert.

rows.reference: Do not rub the eye. Tilt the head with the affected eye down and pour clean water or saline from the inner corner outward to flush it out. If visible on the white of the eye, lift it away with the damp corner of a clean cloth. If flushing fails or pain persists, cover the eye without pressure and seek care.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a foreign object is visible on the surface and not embedded, gently pull it out with your fingers or a clean, moistened cloth. If it's not visible or if it's embedded, flush the eye with clean water and seek medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If the foreign object is visible and lying on the eye's surface, gently pull it out with your fingers or a clean, moistened cloth. If it is not visible or if it is embedded, use a clean cloth to gently pull the surrounding skin around the eye to expose the object.

rows.reference: Rubbing drives a surface particle deeper into the conjunctiva or cornea, turning a loose object into an embedded one, and abrades the cornea, which is painful and infection-prone. A metal fragment can be pushed through the globe, risking permanent vision loss. Flush gently with water instead.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Rubbing the eye when there's a foreign object can cause further irritation, scratch the cornea, or push the object deeper into the eye, potentially causing serious damage. Always avoid rubbing the eye and seek medical help for safe removal.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Rubbing the eye when there's a foreign object can cause further irritation, scratch the cornea, or push the object deeper into the eye, potentially causing serious damage. Always avoid rubbing the eye and follow proper first aid steps to remove or flush the object.

rows.reference: Transport urgently for: temperature above 40 degrees Celsius; any fever above 38 degrees in an infant under 3 months; a rash that does not fade under pressure, suggesting meningococcal disease; seizure with fever; difficulty waking; difficulty breathing; a very unwell appearance; stiff neck or bulging fontanelle.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs that a child’s fever has become too high and requires immediate medical attention include persistent high fever, confusion, rapid breathing, difficulty breathing, or signs of shock like pale, cold, or clammy skin. In such cases, seek emergency medical help immediately.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs that a child’s fever has become too high and requires immediate medical attention include persistent high fever, confusion, rapid breathing, severe headache, or signs of distress such as pale skin, cold extremities, or unconsciousness. Immediate medical care is essential to prevent complications.

rows.reference: Check for a response. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. If breathing, lay them flat and raise the legs above heart level. Loosen tight clothing. Give nothing to eat or drink. Do not leave them alone. Once conscious, keep them lying down before letting them sit up slowly.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If someone has fainted and fallen to the ground, check for any injuries and ensure they are breathing. If they are not breathing, begin CPR immediately. If they have a pulse, place them in the recovery position and seek medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: For someone who has collapsed and fainted, first check for signs of breathing and pulse. If they are not breathing or have no pulse, begin CPR immediately. Place them in the lateral position, check their airway, and continue CPR until medical help arrives.

rows.reference: Treat it as an emergency. Tilt the head back and lift the chin. If breathing, roll them onto their side into the recovery position and monitor breathing. If breathing stops, start CPR. Note the time of collapse. Do not leave them alone. Evacuate urgently.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If someone who fainted doesn’t regain consciousness within a minute or two, seek immediate medical attention. In the meantime, ensure they are in a safe position and continue to monitor their breathing and pulse.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If someone who has fainted does not recover consciousness within one or two minutes, begin CPR immediately. Continue until medical help arrives or the person shows signs of life.

rows.reference: Do not straighten the arm. Support it in the position found. Make a sling from a triangular bandage or improvised cloth to hold the arm across the chest at about 90 degrees of elbow flexion. Pad bony prominences. Never bandage over the fracture site. Check circulation, sensation and movement in the fingers before and after.
rows.train_prompt_answer: To immobilize a suspected fracture, support the injured arm in a comfortable position, ideally with the hand elevated above the elbow. Use a splint or any available firm object to stabilize the arm and prevent further movement.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Place the casualty in a comfortable position, ideally with the injured arm supported at or above the injury site. Use a splint or any available rigid object to immobilize the arm, ensuring that the fracture is not displaced.

rows.reference: Fracture is more likely with an audible crack or snap; visible deformity or abnormal angulation; crepitus on palpation; severe pain worsening with pressure over the bone; swelling and bruising within minutes; inability to bear weight; numbness or tingling below the injury; or bone visible through the skin. If in doubt, treat as a fracture: immobilise and keep weight off.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs that suggest a fracture may be present include intense pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move the joint, and difficulty bearing weight on the injured limb. If the joint is locked or the bone is visibly displaced, it may be a fracture.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs that suggest a fracture include intense pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move the limb, and the presence of open wounds or bone protruding from the fracture site. In such cases, immobilization and support are essential, and the casualty should be kept still and warm while awaiting medical help.

rows.reference: Sharp bone ends can lacerate arteries, veins and nerves, and forcing the limb can tent the skin and convert a closed fracture to an open one. Forcing a dislocation can trap bone or soft tissue in the joint and permanently compromise its blood supply. Immobilise in the position found, padded. Do not reduce or realign.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Attempting to straighten a fracture or dislocate a limb can cause further damage to the bone, nerves, and blood vessels. It can also lead to increased pain and complications. Always support the limb in its current position and seek immediate medical attention.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Attempting to straighten a fracture or dislocate a joint can cause further damage to the bone, nerves, and blood vessels. Immobilization is the key to preventing additional injury. Support the limb in its current position and apply ice to reduce swelling.

rows.reference: RICE is Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Rest: stop activity. Ice: a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes every 2 hours for 48 hours, never directly on skin. Compression: a firm elastic bandage, checking circulation to fingers or toes. Elevation: raise the limb above heart level. Not for fractures, dislocations or open wounds.
rows.train_prompt_answer: The RICE method stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. It is used to treat minor injuries such as sprains, strains, and cuts. It involves applying ice to the injured area to reduce swelling, rest the injured area, and elevate it above heart level to reduce blood flow to the area. It is particularly useful for minor injuries that do not require professional medical attention.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: The RICE method stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. It is used to treat injuries such as sprains, fractures, or burns. It involves applying ice to the injured area to reduce swelling, rest the injured area, and elevate it above the level of the heart to reduce pain and promote healing.

rows.reference: Stop the activity and have the person sit or lie down. Stretch the calf by pulling the toes and ball of the foot toward the shin, holding steadily without forcing. Do not massage hard during the cramp. If the calf is swollen and tender, seek assessment for deep vein thrombosis.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If someone is experiencing a cramp in their calves, have them sit down and rest. Encourage them to relax and stretch their legs gently. If the cramp persists or worsens, apply ice to the affected area and seek medical attention if the cramp lasts for an extended period or worsens.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If someone is experiencing a cramp in their leg, have them sit down and rest. To help alleviate the cramp, they should gently stretch the affected leg by pulling the toes upward. If the cramp persists, apply ice to the affected area and massage the muscle to help relax it.

rows.reference: Lower them to the ground. Do not restrain them. Do not put anything in their mouth. Clear hard objects away and put something soft under the head. Note the time it starts. When convulsions stop, roll them onto their side into the recovery position and monitor breathing. Seek assessment for a first seizure, one over 5 minutes, or failure to return to normal awareness.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If someone who is suddenly standing begins to have convulsions, place them in the lateral position to prevent choking, check their airway, and begin CPR if necessary. Call emergency services immediately and provide further instructions.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If someone is standing suddenly and begins having a tonic-fulseonic seizure, place them in the lateral position to prevent choking, check their airway, and begin CPR if necessary. Continue CPR until medical help arrives.

rows.reference: After a concussion the brain has reduced blood flow and impaired energy regulation. Exertion raises metabolic demand exactly when the brain cannot meet it, prolonging symptoms. A second impact before the first resolves can cause second-impact syndrome, a rapid and potentially fatal brain swelling. Resume only through a graduated protocol after a symptom-free period.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Returning to sport or activity too soon after a concussion can lead to a second impact, causing further damage to the brain and increasing the risk of complications such as a second concussion or further injury. It is crucial to allow the brain to heal and recover before resuming physical activity.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Returning to sport or activity too soon after a concussion can lead to a second impact, causing further damage to the brain. It is crucial to allow the brain to heal and recover before resuming physical activity.

rows.reference: Hypoglycaemia develops over minutes: pale sweaty skin, shakiness, confusion, hunger, palpitations, glucose below 4 mmol/L. Hyperglycaemia develops over hours: heavy thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, fatigue. If unsure and the person is conscious and can swallow safely, give sugar. If they cannot swallow safely, give nothing by mouth. Seek care if no improvement within 15 minutes.
rows.train_prompt_answer: In a conscious person, hypoglycaemic symptoms include sweating, hunger, confusion, slurred speech, and pale, cold, and clammy skin. Hyperglycaemic signs include heavy sweating, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and flushed, warm, and dry skin. Both require immediate sugar intake.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: In a conscious person, hypoglycaemic symptoms include sweating, hunger, confusion, and pale, cold, and clammy skin. In contrast, hyperglycaemic signs include heavy sweating, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and flushed, warm, and dry skin. Both require immediate sugar intake if the person remembers taking insulin.

rows.reference: Warning signs include sudden lightheadedness, pale or ashen skin, cold clammy sweating, nausea, tunnel vision or greying out, a slow weak pulse, ringing in the ears, and leg weakness. These appear 30 seconds to a few minutes before collapse. Get them lying flat and raise their legs.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Early warning signs that a person is about to fainting include feeling dizzy or lightheaded, having a sudden drop in blood pressure, feeling faint or weak, or having a feeling of impending dizziness. These signs should be addressed immediately to prevent fainting.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Early warning signs that a person is about to fainting include feeling dizzy or lightheaded, having a rapid pulse, and feeling faint or weak. The person may also experience nausea, dizziness, or a feeling of impending faintness.

rows.reference: Lean the person forward and give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking the mouth after each. If they fail, give up to 5 chest thrusts: same landmark as CPR compressions, on the lower half of the breastbone, but sharper and slower. Alternate until it clears. If they lose consciousness, start CPR.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a conscious adult cannot speak or breathe, begin CPR immediately. If they are turning blue, perform rescue breaths. If they become unconscious, place them in the lateral position and seek medical help urgently.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If a conscious adult cannot speak or breathe, begin CPR immediately. If they are turning blue, continue CPR while waiting for medical help. If they become unconscious, place them in the lateral position and check for breathing.

rows.reference: Keep them calm and upright, leaning slightly forward. Do not lay them flat. Give 4 puffs of the blue reliever every 4 minutes while preparing for evacuation. Do not give sedatives or antihistamines. No response after 4 or more puffs means a life-threatening attack needing hospital treatment. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If multiple doses of reliever inhaler do not help and the person has known asthma, call emergency services immediately and inform them that the person is having an asthma attack. Continue administering 4 puffs every 4 minutes, and continue monitoring their symptoms. If the person becomes unconscious or their condition worsens, begin CPR and seek emergency medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If someone with known Asthma has an attack and has not received any immediate help, administer 4 puffs of their reliever inhalator and continue giving 2 puffs every 4 minutes until help arrives or the person shows signs of improvement.

rows.reference: An unconscious person loses the reflexes that stop the tongue obstructing the airway and stop vomit being inhaled. Lying on the side with the top knee bent forward and the head tilted back keeps the airway open and lets fluid drain. Do not use it if spinal injury is suspected unless the airway cannot be maintained otherwise.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Placing an unconscious but still breathing person in a recovery position helps maintain their airway open and reduces the risk of aspiration if they vomit. It also helps keep their head and neck supported, which is essential for breathing and preventing further injury.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Placing an unconscious but still breathing person in a recovery position helps maintain their airway open, reduces the risk of aspiration, and allows fluids to drain from the mouth, which is important for preventing choking or aspiration pneumonia.

rows.reference: Start CPR if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally after removal from the water. Agonal gasping is not normal breathing. Coughing, spluttering or movement means they are breathing: monitor closely, as deterioration can be delayed. Anyone rescued needs medical assessment even if apparently recovered. For drowning, give 5 rescue breaths before compressions.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs that a person requires CPR include lack of breathing or irregular breathing, unconsciousness, inability to respond to simple commands, or persistent unresponsiveness despite initial attempts at rescue. In such cases, immediate CPR should be initiated to maintain blood flow and oxygen to vital organs.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs that a person requires CPR include persistent or labored breathing, lack of pulse, bluish lips or face, and inability to rise on their own. If these signs are present, begin CPR immediately while waiting for professional help.

rows.reference: Apply pressure immobilisation immediately. Do not wash the bite: residual venom identifies the species and determines the antivenom. Starting at the toes, wrap a firm elastic or crepe bandage upward over the whole limb, as firmly as for a sprain. Add a second bandage as far up the limb as possible and splint with rigid material. The person must not walk. Evacuate urgently for antivenom; the bandage stays on until hospital.
rows.train_prompt_answer: For a suspected snakebite on the lower limb, apply pressure immobilization bandaging to the affected limb. This helps to immobilize the limb and reduce movement, which can slow down the spread of venom. Ensure that the bandage is not too tight, as this can restrict circulation.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Apply pressure immobilzation bandaging to the lower leg if the victim has a suspected snakebite. This helps to immobilize the limb and reduce movement, which can slow down the spread of venom. Ensure that the bandage is firm but not too tight, and check the victim's breathing and pulse regularly.

rows.reference: Flood the sting with undiluted vinegar immediately for at least 30 seconds. Do not rub the area, apply fresh water, or handle tentacles bare-handed; each triggers further venom release. Remove tentacles with tweezers or gloved hands after the vinegar. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR at once.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If stung by a Box Jellyfish, rinse the affected area with vinegar to neutralize the venom. Do not rub the area, and seek immediate medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If stung by a Box Jellyfish, rinse the affected area with vinegar to neutralize the venom, remove any tentacles, and immerse the sting site in hot water (as hot as the person can tolerate). Seek urgent medical help, as the venom can cause severe pain and complications.

rows.reference: Cutting and sucking remove negligible venom while causing tissue damage and infection risk. Washing removes the residual venom used to identify the species, which determines the antivenom given. A tourniquet causes ischaemic damage while doing nothing to stop spread, because Australian snake venom travels via the lymphatic system. Pressure immobilisation is the only evidence-based first aid.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Cutting, sucking, or washing the wound can cause more harm than good. Applying a tourniQUET complicates the situation and increases the risk of further injury.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Cutting, sucking, or washing the wound can cause more harm than good. Applying a tourniquette can restrict circulation and worsen the injury. Washing the wound can introduce bacteria and delay proper treatment.

rows.reference: Heat stroke is life-threatening. Recognise it by core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius, hot dry skin, confusion or unconsciousness, and a rapid strong pulse. Move to the coolest place and remove excess clothing. Cool at once: ice packs to neck, armpits and groin; wet the skin and fan vigorously; or immerse in cool water if safe. Give no fluids to anyone confused or unconscious. Begin cooling within minutes.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Heat stroke occurs when the body becomes extremely hot due to prolonged exposure to high temperatures. Symptoms include confusion, rapid pulse, hot, dry skin, and a body temperature of over 40°C. Immediate action is required: move the person to a cool place, loosen their clothing, and cool them down with ice packs or cool water.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs of heat stroke include confusion, rapid pulse, hot, dry skin, and a body temperature of over 40°C. Immediate action is required: move the person to a cool place, cool them down with ice packs, and fanning them. Do not give them water or food.

rows.reference: Cool the burn under cool running water for a full 20 minutes immediately. Do not use ice, iced water, butter, toothpaste or creams. Then cover loosely with clean non-fluffy material such as cling film. Do not wrap tightly or burst blisters. Remove rings and tight clothing before swelling begins, unless stuck to the wound. Seek hospital assessment.
rows.train_prompt_answer: For a partial thickness (1/4 to 2/3 of the total) burn covering a large area of the forearm, apply a sterile, non-adherent dressing to the burn area. This helps protect the wound from further damage and reduces pain. Cover the burn with a sterile, nonstick dressing and secure it with a firm bandage.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: For a partial thickness (1/4 to 1/2 the burn area) burn on the forearm, apply a sterile, non-adherent dressing directly to the burn site. This helps protect the wound from further damage and reduces infection risk. Cover the dressing with a clean, non-fluffy cloth to prevent further injury.

rows.reference: Butter, oils and toothpaste trap heat in burned tissue and block the cooling running water provides. They also feed bacteria, raising infection risk. Ice constricts vessels at the burn margins, reducing blood flow to tissue that might survive, and risks frostbite. Cool running water for 20 minutes is the only evidence-based treatment.
rows.train_prompt_answer: These materials can trap heat, cause further irritation, or worsen the injury. They can also interfere with proper wound care and increase the risk of infection.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Applying these materials can trap heat, cause further irritation, or introduce contaminants like bacteria into the wound. They should be avoided unless no other options exist.

rows.reference: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion and fatigue, resembling flu without fever. Several people or pets affected in the same space suggests it. Do not enter without breathing apparatus. Move the person to fresh air if safe. Monitor breathing, as effects can worsen after apparent recovery. If unresponsive, start CPR.
rows.train_prompt_answer: Signs of carbon monoxide exposure include headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, confusion, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing. If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning, immediately move the person to fresh air, check their airway, breathing, and pulse, and seek emergency medical help.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: Signs of carbon monoxide exposure include dizziness, headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing. If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning, immediately move the person to fresh air, check their airway, and start CPR if necessary. Seek medical help urgently.

rows.reference: Do not induce vomiting. Note any medication containers. Keep the person awake and talking. If they become drowsy, roll them onto their side into the recovery position. Give nothing to eat or drink. Monitor breathing. If breathing stops or becomes abnormal, start CPR. Transport urgently with all containers.
rows.train_prompt_answer: If a conscious person takes an overdose of any medication, it is important to stay calm and assess their condition. If they are breathing normally and have no signs of severe injury, you can try to contact emergency services for further guidance. If they lose consciousness or show signs of distress, you should seek immediate medical attention.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: If the person is conscious and confused, keep them calm and still. Offer reassurance and avoid giving them anything to eat or drink. Place them in the lateral position and monitor their breathing and pulse closely. If their condition worsens, seek emergency medical help immediately.

rows.reference: Do not move a suspected spinal injury casualty unless there is immediate danger to life. If movement is unavoidable, one person holds the head in neutral alignment with the spine. Use a log-roll with a minimum of three rescuers: one controls the head, two roll the body as one rigid unit. Do not sit or stand the casualty.
rows.train_prompt_answer: When moving a casualty with a suspected spinal injury, it is crucial to support the head, neck, and spine at all times. Use your hands to gently guide the casualty, ensuring that the head remains aligned with the spine. Avoid twisting or bending the body, as this can cause further damage.
rows.offline_prompt_answer: When moving a casualty with a suspected spinal injury, it is crucial to support the head, neck, and spine at all times. Move the casualty slowly and gently, using your hands or a piece of soft material like a jacket or rug. Avoid twisting or bending the body, as this could cause further damage to the spine.
